opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think Arc should be a place that does things that are really hard to do anywhere else. Biomedical research has a structural problem. Academic labs run on short grant cycles and are built around individual PIs and the trainees who come through for a few years. Companies have to answer to near-term commercial milestones. A lot of the most important problems fall into the gap between them. They need long time horizons, big interdisciplinary teams, and serious infrastructure, but they aren't yet a product.

So Arc's role, as I see it, is to fill that gap. We give scientists flexible, long-term funding so they can pursue curiosity-driven ideas without writing grants all the time. Then we pair that with technology centers in areas like genome engineering, multi-omics, cell biology and imaging, and especially machine learning, that no single lab could build or maintain alone.

The thing I'm most excited about is the convergence of AI and biology. We can now generate data at enormous scale and train models that learn the language of DNA, RNA and proteins. Our Evo models trained on genomic sequence are one example. Our virtual cell efforts, which try to predict how cells respond to perturbations, are another. The goal is to move biology from a mostly descriptive science toward a predictive, even designable one. And for complex diseases like neurodegeneration, cancer and immune dysfunction, that shift could matter enormously.

Ultimately, we want Arc to be an experiment in how science itself is organized. If we can show that a different model accelerates discovery, that's valuable beyond any single paper. Other institutions can borrow the parts that work. We also put a lot of emphasis on openness: releasing models, datasets and tools so the broader community can build on them. If we're successful, Arc won't just produce great science. It'll help change how great science gets done.

r001.rationale: The response presents Arc as filling a gap with long-term funding and shared infrastructure to enable hard biological research and advance biology toward predictive, designable capabilities.

r002.rationale: It contrasts academic research with company timelines and discusses AI’s role in biology, but does not compare where major mechanistic or basic-science breakthroughs occur in biology versus AI or computer science.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about Arc is that we started it because we felt there was a gap in how biology actually gets done. On one side you have academic labs, which are incredibly creative but are organized around a PI and a handful of trainees, with a funding cycle that rewards short-term, incremental projects. On the other side you have industry, which has scale and engineering discipline but is necessarily pointed at a product and a timeline. A lot of the most important problems in biology fall in between. They need long horizons, real engineering investment, and teams bigger than a single lab, but they're too early or too fundamental to be a company.

So the role we try to play is to be that middle institution. We give investigators long-term, no-strings funding so they're not writing grants every year, and we pair that with centralized technology platforms, things like genome engineering, sequencing, and increasingly computation and machine learning, run by professional scientists and engineers whose job is to build infrastructure, not to publish a first-author paper. Those two pieces together let you take on projects that otherwise just don't happen.

The second thing I'd say is that we think the most important thing happening in biology right now is that it's becoming a data and computation problem. For a long time the bottleneck was measurement. Now we can generate enormous datasets, and the question is whether we can actually learn the underlying rules from them. We've been building large biological foundation models, trained on genomes across the tree of life, and the goal there is not to beat a benchmark. It's to see whether a model can start to capture something like a working understanding of how sequence maps to function, so that eventually you can design and predict rather than just screen and observe.

And the third piece is disease focus. Arc is organized around hard problems, things like neurodegeneration, immune dysfunction, and complex diseases where the field has been stuck for decades. We want our technologies and models to be pointed at those, with the expectation that if we're successful, some of what we build gets spun out, open-sourced, or otherwise handed off to people who can take it the rest of the way. I don't think Arc should try to do everything. I think it should try to do the things that nobody else is structurally set up to do, and then make those capabilities broadly available.

r001.rationale: The response presents Arc’s purpose as taking on biology projects that need long horizons and substantial research infrastructure, including building capabilities to understand and predict biological function.

r002.rationale: It contrasts academic labs with industry and discusses biology’s growing computational focus, but it does not compare where major biological breakthroughs occur with the pattern in AI or computer science.

astra-6.text:
I think Arc should be a place where scientists can pursue important questions that don’t fit neatly into the way research is usually funded or organized. Biology is full of problems that require sustained effort, collaboration across disciplines, and a willingness to try things that might fail. We want to give people the freedom and support to do that.

There’s also an opportunity to bring discovery and technology development closer together. A new tool can let you ask a question that was previously inaccessible, and a biological discovery can reveal what tools you need next. Having those efforts in close conversation can be incredibly productive.

Ultimately, I’d want Arc’s impact to extend well beyond the institute itself—through discoveries, tools, and approaches that help the broader scientific community understand biology and, over time, turn that understanding into better treatments for disease.

r001.rationale: The response discusses pursuing important questions and supporting sustained effort, but it does not clearly identify long-term breakthroughs in biological research capabilities as Arc Institute’s purpose.

r002.rationale: It does not compare where major mechanistic or basic-science breakthroughs in biology occur with the pattern in AI or computer science.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Arc should be a place where scientists can pursue ambitious, long-term questions and have the support to really go after them. In biology, an enormous amount of energy goes into securing funding, building a lab, and assembling the tools you need before you can even test an idea. We want to give people more room to focus on the science.

And then there’s an opportunity to do things together that would be very difficult for any individual lab: build new technologies, generate useful datasets, and bring experimental biology and computation into a much tighter loop. The goal is to help us understand how cells work well enough that we can predict what happens when we perturb them—and eventually turn that understanding into better treatments for disease.

If Arc succeeds, the impact should extend well beyond the institute through the discoveries, tools, and people it contributes to the broader scientific community.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes supporting ambitious, long-term biological questions and building technologies and datasets to understand and predict cell behavior, identifying long-term advances in biological research capabilities as Arc’s purpose.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare where biology breakthroughs occur with the pattern in AI or computer science.
